KEY MESSAGE 1...
A digging trough will evolve into a strong, closed upper low as
it dives through the Mississippi River Valley tonight before
becoming more vertically stacked over the Upper Ohio Valley on
Thursday. Notable diffluent flow downstream will result in
pretty rapid intensification of a developing surface low across
the Carolinas that will track north through our area and
eventually occlude beneath the upper low. A tight surface 
gradient between the low and a high positioned near Maine, 
coupled with an anomalously strong low-level jet in exceedance 
of 99th percentile climatology, will result in windy conditions
on Thanksgiving. Latest runs of both the NBM and REFS have 
broadened their footprint for stronger wind gusts with higher 
probabilities expanding farther west. This is likely being 
driven by two primary factors:

The first being an increased likelihood of breaking mountain 
waves spilling farther west/ridgetops being within the core of 
the LLJ. In the PA & WV ridges, REFS probability for High Wind 
Warning criteria gusts >58 mph is 80-100%, >70 mph 50-75%, and 
>80 mph around 10% as these ridgetops sit solidly within the 
core of the 70-80 knot jet. The High Wind Warning has been
expanded to cover all of our higher elevation zones. Farther 
west, swaths of REFS probability for Advisory criteria gusts >46
mph are up to 80% into Indiana, Jefferson, Westmoreland, and 
Fayette Counties. The Advisory has been expanded there. Still 
wouldn't rule out those gusts even farther west where REFS 
probability has increased into Butler, Allegheny, Washington, 
and Greene Counties, though have less confidence there, and have
held off on further expansion at this time. In fact, those 
areas might be driven by the second factor...

The second factor is more resultant of mixing than downslope 
wind or residence within the LLJ core. Near-surface thermal 
profiles aren't necessarily stable as much as they are 
isothermal or moist adiabatic at times within a saturated 
boundary layer. This could allow for a coincident occurrence of 
higher wind gusts mixing down within the heaviest rain. In 
general, expect that peak easterly wind gusts will range from 
35-45 mph in the lower elevations. The window of impact starts 
first around Preston/Tucker Counties before shifting north 
through the morning/afternoon coincident with the shift of the 
low-level jet placement.

Wind subsides during the late afternoon/evening hours as the
surface low pivots and begins lifting northeast, though gusts
will continue in the ridges. Another round of gusty winds 
develop after the low exits in the post-frontal environment 
(veering to the WSW in the process and thus lessening the
downslope enhancement locally) Friday, and probabilities for 
reaching Advisory criteria are mainly confined to eastern Tucker
County.

KEY MESSAGE 2...
The aforementioned low pressure system will draw upon Atlantic
waters to result in widespread rain for a large portion of the
day Thursday into Friday morning; any breaks in activity will be
primarily due to temporary mid-level dry slotting that develops
near/east of I-79 as well as partial rain shadow effects from
the downsloping east winds (and the drying effect it causes). As
such, there will likely be a minimum in rain amounts along the
western slope of the higher elevation in PA down to WV.
Conversely, a pivoting, stronger area of 850-700 mb
frontogenesis is likely to drive a narrow area of higher 
amounts in eastern OH. Where exactly this sets up is still a bit
uncertain, and could be as far east as the WV Panhandle to as 
far west as Zanesville. REFS LPPM bumps up to 2"+ in that area, 
so while spatial uncertainty remains, overall confidence in 
these amounts somewhere in that area is increasing. The heaviest
rain is likely in the morning hours with tapering intensity into
the afternoon. Areawide, there's a 80-100% probability of >1"
save the aforementioned rain shadowed area. >2" probability is
confined to that area of eastern OH where the heavier axis will
set up. Flood concern is still expected to be low as the rates
are low chance to reach flash flood guidance.

As the surface low lifts northeast out of the region through the
day Friday, modest cold advection at the surface and aloft will
allow for periods of snow to mix in with the rain at lower
elevations (or change precip to all snow in the higher
elevations). Steepening lapse rates plus some lake influences
also favors precipitation being more shower-y in nature and
result in the "on and off" precipitation occurrence intervals.
For the lower elevations, the lack of colder air aloft (850mb
temps bottom out to only -2 celsius) plus above-freezing surface
temps ensures any flakes that fall immediately melt (or don't
stick during overnight hours). For the higher elevations, light
accumulations generally less than 2" can't be ruled out but even
scenarios showcasing 3"+ may be deceiving as daytime temps allow
for some melting between show
